findings.quote: It is bonded to one hydrogen and one carbon group.
findings.problem: The aldehyde definition fails at its boundary case. Methanal (formaldehyde), HCHO, is the simplest aldehyde, but its carbonyl carbon is bonded to two hydrogens and no carbon group. With this definition, and with Example 7's test 'One hydrogen on it means an aldehyde', a student cannot classify methanal, because it fits neither the aldehyde nor the ketone definition. The general fact is that the carbonyl carbon carries at least one hydrogen.
findings.source: IUPAC Gold Book, 'aldehydes': RC(=O)H, where R may be H; checklist B01 and the reader-rules boundary test (Sol audit)

findings.quote: A hydrogen bond is an attraction between a hydrogen attached to oxygen or nitrogen and an oxygen or nitrogen on another molecule.
findings.problem: This is given as a general definition but leaves out fluorine. HF is the standard exception: it forms hydrogen bonds although the definition excludes it. The sibling lesson content/lessons/science/chemistry/chemical-bonding.md teaches 'hydrogen bonded to N, O, or F'. A student who uses this definition would wrongly say HF has no hydrogen bonding, and the two lessons contradict each other.
findings.source: IUPAC 2011 definition of the hydrogen bond (Arunan et al., Pure Appl. Chem. 83, 1637); chemical-bonding.md line 96; checklist B01

findings.quote: Lipids are not all fats and oils, and not all are polymers.
findings.problem: 'Not all are polymers' tells the student that some lipids are polymers. Standard biology teaches that lipids are the one major biomolecule class that does not form true polymers, which is a common test item on biomolecules (upcat-L161, dcat-L079 at curriculum class). The sentence leads to the wrong answer.
findings.source: Campbell Biology, Chapter 5 (lipids do not include true polymers); brief requirement rows upcat-L161 and dcat-L079; checklist B01

findings.quote: For a carbonyl, ask whether the $C=O$ carbon has a hydrogen on it. If yes, it is an aldehyde.
findings.problem: The shortcut is given for any carbonyl, and the lesson says the carbonyl group also appears in carboxylic acids and esters. It has no stated limit. Methanoic (formic) acid, HCOOH, and formate esters have a hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon, so this test would wrongly call them aldehydes. The shortcut should say it only separates aldehydes from ketones, once acids and esters are ruled out.
findings.source: Checklist L27; writer-rules 'Rules added after round 1' item 4 (word every shortcut with its limit)
